'''Douglas M. Warhit''' {{born|28|April|1955}} is the actor who played [[Kazago]] in the {{s|TNG}} [[TNG Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|The Battle}}. For this role, he was credited simply as '''Doug Warhit'''. He has an undergraduate degree from New York University and a masters degree from Antioch University in Ohio.

He made his feature film acting debut in {{wt|The Chosen (1981 film)|The Chosen}} (1984, featuring ''Next Generation'' writer [[Stuart Charno]]). He followed this film with small roles in {{wt|Private School (film)|Private School}}, with [[Ray Walston]], and {{wt|Christine (1983 film)|Christine}}, co-starring [[Bruce French]] and Stuart Charno. He was then seen in {{wt|Body Double}} (1984), starring [[Craig Wasson]] and [[Gregg Henry]], and had a supporting role in {{wt|Toy Soldiers (1984 film)|Toy Soldiers}} that same year. The latteralso featured [[Tracy Scoggins]] in the cast.

Warhit's subsequent film credits include [[Paramount Pictures]]' {{wt|Beverly Hills Cop}} (1984, starring [[Eddie Murphy]], [[Jonathan Banks]], [[Steven Berkoff]], [[Michael Champion]] and [[Ronny Cox]]) and {{wt|Playing for Keeps (1986 film)|Playing for Keeps}} (1989, with [[Timothy Carhart]]). His most recent film was {{wt|Look Who's Talking Too}} (1990, starring [[Kirstie Alley]]).

Prior to his role on ''The Next Generation'', Warhit made appearances on such television shows as {{wt|Remington Steele}} (starring [[Pierce Brosnan]], with [[James Read]]), {{wt|Airwolf}} (1985, with [[Joseph Ruskin]]), ''The Facts of Life'' (with [[Paul Comi]]), {{wt|Misfits of Science}} (with [[Meg Wyllie]]), {{wt|You Again?}} (with [[Sam Anderson]]), {{wt|Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting}} (with [[Marshall R. Teague]]), and {{wt|The Wizard (TV series)|The Wizard}} (starring [[David Rappaport]], with [[Gracie Harrison]]). Following ''The Next Generation'', Warhit was seen in the pilot episode of {{wt|China Beach}}, starring [[Robert Picardo]], [[Jeff Kober]], [[Tim Ryan]] and [[Concetta Tomei]]. [[James Cromwell]] also appeared in the pilot episode.

Warhit later appeared on two episodes of {{wt|Civil Wars (TV series)|Civil Wars}} (with [[Jeff Allin]], [[Richard Fancy]], [[Aaron Lustig]] and [[Ken Thorley]]) and {{wt|NYPD Blue}} (1996, starring [[Gordon Clapp]] and [[Sharon Lawrence]], with [[Anne Haney]]). He was last seen in an episode of [[Paramount Television]]'s {{wt|Clueless (TV series)|Clueless}}, starring [[Wallace Shawn]], in 1996.

Today, Warhit is semi-retired from acting and teaches acting to students at various colleges and universities and in his own private time. He has been teaching on-camera cold reading and scene study and coaching actors for auditions for over twenty years. He is also a licensed psychotherapist and life coach.

'''Robert Towers''' {{born|19|August|1936}} is the actor who portrayed the [[Rata]] in the {{s|TNG}} [[TNG Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|The Battle}}. He was born in New York City, New York. He also voiced three characters in the {{video game}} ''{{dis|Star Trek: 25th Anniversary|PC}}'', credited as '''Bob Towers'''.

Towers' career has been focused mainly in comedy and family films with some action roles mixed in. Towers co-starred in {{wt|Stewardess School}} (1986, with [[Earl Boen]], [[Brett Cullen]], [[Paddi Edwards]], [[Paul Eiding]], [[Bill Erwin]], [[Richard Lineback]] and [[Don Most]]) and {{wt|Masters of the Universe (1987 film)|Masters of the Universe}} (1988, starring [[Frank Langella]], with {{s|VOY}}{{'}}s [[Robert Duncan McNeill]], [[Anthony De Longis]], [[Meg Foster]] and [[Christina Pickles]]). Towers was later seen in {{wt|Hot to Trot}} (1988, with [[Virginia Madsen]], [[Jim Metzler]] and [[Vyto Ruginis]]), and {{wt|Let It Ride (film)|Let it Ride}} (1989, with [[Terri Garr]] and [[Michelle Phillips]]). In the 90s Towers appeared in {{wt|Switch (1991 film)|Switch}} (1991, with [[James Harper]] and [[Lily Mariye]]). Towers later appear in ''[[Sarah Silverman]]: Jesus is Magic'' (2005). He was also in {{wt|The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (film)|The Curious Case of Benjamin Button}} (2007). In 2009, Towers acted in ''Table for Three'' with [[Jennifer Morrison]]. He later appeared as Lou in {{wt|The Wedding Ringer}} (2015).

On television Towers kept active. He appeared on ''Baretta'' guest-starring with [[Jerry Hardin]] in "The Appointment", however Towers' television resume only expanded as time went on. Towers worked with [[Bonita Friedericy]] on {{wt|Angel (1999 TV series)|Angel}}. He also appeared on ''[[Frasier]]'' (2004, starring [[Kelsey Grammer]], with [[Larry Cedar]] and [[Don McManus]]), {{wt|Hannah Montana}} (2009 & 2011, former with [[Michael Kagan]]) {{wt|It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia}} (2007).

He later appeared in {{wt|Raven's Home}} (2017) and {{wt|Bunk'd}} (2018, starring [[Peyton List]]).

'''Clarence Williams III''' {{born|21|August|1939|died|4|June|2021}} was the Tony Award-nominated actor who played [[Omet'iklan]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 4|fourth season]] episode {{e|To the Death}}. He is perhaps best known for his role as "Linc Hayes" on the 1970s television series ''The Mod Squad'', co-starring [[Tige Andrews]], and produced by [[Harve Bennett]].

Born in New York City, Williams was the grandson of legendary musician {{w|Clarence Williams (musician)|Clarence Williams}} and blues singer {{w|Eva Taylor}}. Williams became interested in drama as a teenager and began pursuing an acting career following a two-year stint in the United States Air Force. He started performing in stage productions, ultimately working his way to the Broadway stage in 1960 with a role in a short-lived play called ''The Long Dream''. He also broke into feature films, making his debut in the medium with an uncredited appearance in the 1959 war drama ''Pork Chop Hill'', which also featured [[Biff Elliot]], [[Barry Atwater]], [[Ken Lynch]], [[Paul Comi]], and [[Bert Remsen]].

From November 1964 through February 1965, Williams starred in the Broadway production of ''Slow Dance on the Killing Ground''. His performance in this play earned him a 1965 Tony Award nomination as Best Featured Actor in a Play. He also won the 1965 Theatre World Award for his performance. Three years later, he won the role of the afro-wearing "Linc Hayes" on ''The Mod Squad''. He remained with the show for all five seasons, ending in 1973. He reprised the role in 1979 for the TV movie ''Return of the Mod Squad''. Later that year, Williams returned to the Broadway stage to co-star with [[Dwight Schultz]] in ''Night and Day'', which ran for 95 performances, ending in 1980.

It was during the 1980s that Williams began to appear in more films and television shows. He guest-starred in two episodes of {{wt|T. J. Hooker}} starring [[William Shatner]], [[James Darren]], and [[Richard Herd]]. Williams also made guest appearances on the TV shows {{wt|Hill Street Blues}} (1984, with [[Barbara Bosson]] and [[James B. Sikking]]), {{wt|WThe Cosby Show}} (1985, with [[Sabrina Le Beauf]]), and {{wt|Miami Vice}} (1985, directed by [[Michael O'Herlihy]] and starring [[Edward James Olmos]]). His film credits during the 1980s included ''52 Pick-Up'' (1986, with [[John Glover]] and [[Alex Henteloff]]), {{wt|Tough Guys Don't Dance (film)|Tough Guys Don't Dance}} (1987, with [[Lawrence Tierney]]), and {{wt|I'm Gonna Git You Sucka}} (1988, with [[Bernie Casey]]). He also played the father of Prince's character, "The Kid", in {{wt|Purple Rain (film)|Purple Rain}} (1984).

Throughout the 1990s, Williams was seen on such shows as {{wt|Twin Peaks}} (1990, co-starring [[Mädchen Amick]], [[Richard Beymer]], [[Catherine Coulson]], [[Joan Chen]], [[Tony Jay]] and [[Kenneth Welsh]]), ''Tales from the Crypt'' (1992, with [[Salome Jens]]), and {{wt|Walker, Texas Ranger}} (1997, starring [[Clarence Gilyard, Jr.]] and [[Noble Willingham]]). His appearance on {{wt|Millennium (TV series)|Millennium}} (starring [[Lance Henriksen]], [[Megan Gallagher]] and [[Terry O'Quinn]]) earned him an Image Award nomination in 1998, as did his role in the film ''Hoodlum'' (1997, with [[Mike Starr]] and [[Vanessa Williams]]). His other film projects during the 1990s included {{wt|My Heroes Have Always Been Cowboys (film)|My Heroes Have Always Been Cowboys}} (1991, with [[Megan Parlen]]), {{wt|Deep Cover}} (1992, starring [[Laurence Fishburne]], with [[Gregory Sierra]]), {{wt|Tales from the Hood}} (1995, starring [[Corbin Bernsen]]), {{wt|The Brave (film)|The Brave}} (1997, with [[Iggy Pop]] and [[Azalea Davila]]), {{wt|Frogs for Snakes}} (1998, with [[Ron Perlman]] and Mike Starr), {{wt|Half-Baked}} (1998), and {{wt|The General's Daughter (film)|The General's Daughter}} (1999, co-starring [[James Cromwell]]). 

Some of Williams' later TV appearances include episodes of {{wt|Law & Order}} and {{wt|Judging Amy}}. Between 2005 and 2007, Williams starred as Philby in Hallmark's ''Mystery Woman'' series of made-for-TV movies. As for his later film work, both Williams and fellow ''Deep Space Nine'' actress [[Rosalind Chao]] made uncredited appearances in {{wt|Impostor (2001 film)|Imposter}} (2001), which also featured [[Brian Brophy]]. In 2004, Williams starred with [[David Clennon]], [[Alec Newman]], [[Zoe Saldana]], and [[Gabrielle Union]] in {{wt|Constellation (film)|Constellation}}. Williams played the Harlem gangster Bumpy Johnson in {{wt|American Gangster (film)|American Gangster}} (2007, with [[Chiwetel Ejiofor]], [[Kathleen Garrett]], [[Idris Elba]], [[Joe Morton]] and [[Jon Polito]]).

He died of colon cancer on 4 June 2021.

'''Andrew Hawkes''' {{born|11|June|1966}} is the actor who played [[Amat'igan]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 4|fourth season]] episode {{e|Broken Link}}.

Hawkes' first motion picture role came in 1996's ''Kounterfeit'', in which he played Tommy 'Hopscotch' Hopkins; {{s|TNG}} guest star [[Corbin Bernsen]] played Marty Hopkins in the movie.

In 1998 he starred in ''Sinbad: The Battle of the Dark Knights'' with [[Dean Stockwell]] and [[Anthony De Longis]]. A year later, he starred in two movies, ''Interceptors'' and ''The Hunter's Moon''. [[Brad Dourif]] also starred in the former, while Hawkes' fellow ''Deep Space Nine'' guest star [[Charles Napier]] starred in the latter. 

In 2001, he starred in ''Contagion'', along with [[Megan Gallagher]], [[Jeffrey Combs]] and [[Tom Wright]]. He also guest-starred in {{wt|24 (TV series)|24}} with [[Gregory Itzin]], [[Jude Ciccolella]], [[Stephanie Erb]] and Tom Wright), ''Without a Trace'' (with [[K Callan]]), ''Dexter'' and ''Community''.

'''Marshall R. Teague''' {{born|16|April|1953}} is the actor who played [[Temo'Zuma]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 4|fourth season]] episode {{e|Hippocratic Oath}}, where he was credited as '''Marshall Teague'''. He later played [[Haluk]] in the {{s|VOY}} [[VOY Season 3|third season]] episode {{e|Distant Origin}}.

== Further career ==
He has also guest-starred on {{wt|Quantum Leap (1989 TV series)|Quantum Leap}} (1989, starring [[Scott Bakula]] and [[Dean Stockwell]],  with [[Lance LeGault]]), ''[[Babylon 5]]'' (starring [[Claudia Christian]], [[Andreas Katsulas]], [[Bill Mumy]], [[Mary Kay Adams]], [[Robin Sachs]], [[Patricia Tallman]], and [[John Vickery]]), {{wt|Sliders (TV series)|Sliders}} (starring [[Jerry O'Connell]]), and ''[[Stargate SG-1]]'' (1998, starring [[Richard Dean Anderson]] and [[Michael Shanks]]). He also made appearances on {{wt|The A-Team}} (1985, starring [[Dwight Schultz]]), {{wt|MacGyver (1985 TV series)|MacGyver}} (starring Richard Dean Anderson), {{wt|Renegade (TV series)|Renegade}} (1995, with [[Branscombe Richmond]], [[Ken Olandt]], and [[Cynthia Madvig]]), and {{wt|Walker, Texas Ranger}} (starring [[Clarence Gilyard, Jr.]] and [[Noble Willingham]]), and had a recurring role as Marine Colonel Douglas Drayton on ''Pensacola: Wings of Gold''.

He also appeared in {{wt|The Rock (film)|The Rock}} (1996, with [[Tony Todd]] and [[Tom Towles]]) and {{wt|Armageddon (1998 film)|Armageddon}} (1998, with [[Lawrence Tierney]] and [[Jason Isaacs]]). His other film credits include {{wt|Road House (1989 film)|Road House}} (1989, with [[Anthony De Longis]], [[Kevin Tighe]], and [[Tiny Ron]]) and ''Crime and Punishment in Suburbia'' (2000, with [[Brad Greenquist]]). He has also appeared in a number of made-for-TV movies, including {{wt|Starflight: The Plane That Couldn't Land}} (1983, with [[Gail Strickland]] and [[Ellen Bry]]), {{wt|Elvis and Me (miniseries)|Elvis and Me}} (1988, with [[Anne Haney]]), {{wt|Rough Riders (miniseries)|Rough Riders}} (1997, with [[Brian Keith]] and [[Mark Moses]]), {{wt|Crossfire Trail}} (2001, with [[Virginia Madsen]] and [[Patrick Kilpatrick]]), and ''Monte Walsh'' (2003, with [[Wallace Shawn]]).

'''Ed O'Ross''' {{born|5|July|1949}} is the actor who played [[Gaavrin]] in the {{s|ENT}} [[ENT Season 2|second season]] episode {{e|Bounty}}. His costume was later sold off on the [[It's A Wrap! sale and auction]] on eBay. {{stala|4187}}

After a brief career as a boxer and later a minor league baseball player, O'Ross had his acting debut in the 1982 film ''Dear Mr. Wonderful''.

Besides his appearance on ''Enterprise'', O'Ross has been a guest on such television shows as {{wt|Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting}} (1985, with [[Charles Rocket]]), {{wt|Scarecrow and Mrs. King}} (1986, starring [[Kate Jackson]], with [[Robert Picardo]]), {{wt|Murder, She Wrote}} (with [[Monte Markham]] and [[William Windom]]), {{wt|Seinfeld}} (1995 & 1998, with [[Jason Alexander]]), ''[[Frasier]]'' (1997, starring [[Kelsey Grammer]], with [[Jennifer Williams]]), ''Beyond Belief: Fact or Fiction'' (hosted by [[Jonathan Frakes]]), ''The Handler'' (three episodes, including one with [[Armin Shimerman]]), {{wt|NYPD Blue}} (2002, starring [[Gordon Clapp]], with [[Richard Fancy]] and [[Samantha Smith]]), {{wt|Boston Legal}} (starring [[René Auberjonois]] and [[William Shatner]]), and {{wt|Shark (American TV series)|Shark}} (2007, starring [[Jeri Ryan]], with [[Colby French]], [[Ray Proscia]], [[Dakin Matthews]] and [[Albie Selznick]]). However, he is perhaps best known for his recurring role as Nikolai on {{wt|Six Feet Under (TV series)|Six Feet Under}}, on which he worked with fellow ''[[Star Trek]]'' performers [[Ed Begley, Jr.]], [[John Billingsley]], [[Joel Brooks]], [[Joanna Cassidy]], [[Art Chudabala]], [[Bill Cobbs]], [[James Cromwell]], [[Tim de Zarn]], [[Larry Drake]], [[Robert Foxworth]], [[Jenette Goldstein]], [[Graham Jarvis]], [[Stanley Kamel]], [[Leonard Kelly-Young]], [[Richard Lynch]], [[Matt McCoy]], [[Dina Meyer]], [[Robert Pine]], [[Daniel Roebuck]], [[Raphael Sbarge]], [[Wendy Schaal]], [[Barbara J. Tarbuck]], [[Kellie Waymire]], [[Wade Andrew Williams]], and [[Bruce Wright]]. O'Ross also worked alongside {{s|VOY}} star [[Jennifer Lien]] as the voice of Agent K on {{wt|Men in Black: The Series}} during the show's first (1997-98) season.

In film, O'Ross had supporting roles in {{wt|Lethal Weapon}} (1987, with [[Lycia Naff]], [[Mitchell Ryan]], [[Henry Brown]], and [[Jimmie F. Skaggs]]), {{wt|Full Metal Jacket}} (1987), {{wt|Another 48 Hrs.}} (1990, starring [[Eddie Murphy]], with [[Bernie Casey]] and [[Biff Yeager]]), {{wt|Dick Tracy (1990 film)|Dick Tracy}} (1990, with [[Hamilton Camp]], [[Seymour Cassel]], [[Colm Meaney]], [[John Schuck]], [[Kathy Bates]], [[Paul Sorvino]], [[Ian Wolfe]], and [[Michael J. Pollard]]), and {{wt|Universal Soldier (1992 film)|Universal Soldier}} (1992, co-starring [[Tommy "Tiny" Lister, Jr.]] and [[Leon Rippy]]) and ''Play Nice'' (1992 with [[Scott Burkholder]], [[Ron Canada]] and [[Bruce McGill]]). In 1987, he co-starred with [[Michael Nouri]], [[Larry Cedar]], [[William Boyett]], [[Wren T. Brown]], [[Branscombe Richmond]], [[Joey Aresco]], [[Mark Phelan]], and [[Alan Marcus]] in {{wt|The Hidden (1987 film)|The Hidden}} and appeared, along with [[Andrew Robinson]], [[Diane Salinger]], and Armin Shimerman, in the drama ''The Verne Miller Story''. In {{wt|Red Heat (1988 film)|Red Heat}} (1988), O'Ross played the main villain, a Russian drug dealer being chased by star {{w|Arnold Schwarzenegger}}. [[Allan Graf]] served as O'Ross' [[stunt double]] in the film, while [[Joel Kramer]] doubled for Schwarzenegger. The movie also featured [[Michael G. Hagerty]], music by [[James Horner]], and was photographed by [[Matthew F. Leonetti]]. Later films include {{wt|Hoodlum (film)|Hoodlum}} (1997, starring [[Laurence Fishburne]], with [[Mike Starr]], [[Vanessa Williams]] and [[Clarence Williams III]]), {{wt|Mindstorm (film)|Mindstorm}} (2001, with Clarence Williams III), and ''Delta Farce'' (2007, with [[Shelly Desai]] and [[Glenn Morshower]]).

== Other ''Trek'' connections ==
Additional projects in which Ed O'Ross appeared with other ''Star Trek'' performers include:
* {{wt|The Cotton Club (film)|The Cotton Club}} (1984 film, with Bill Cobbs, [[Mark Margolis]] and [[Tucker Smallwood]])

'''Jake Dengel''' {{born|19|June|1933|died|14|November|1994}} was the actor who played [[Mordoc]] in the {{s|TNG}} [[TNG Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|The Last Outpost}}. Archive footage of this appearance was incorporated into the [[TNG Season 2|second season]] episode {{e|Shades of Gray}}.

Dengel's film debut was 1964's ''Twelfth Night'' based on the [[William Shakespeare]] play. In the 1980s, Dengel appeared in {{wt|Ragtime (film)|Ragtime}} (1981, with {{dis|John Anderson|actor}}, [[Josh Clark]], [[Brad Dourif]], [[Jim Fitzpatrick]], [[Robert Joy]], [[Andreas Katsulas]], [[Ethan Phillips]], and [[Edward Wiley]]), {{wt|Something Wicked This Way Comes (film)|Something Wicked This Way Comes}} (1983, with [[Ellen Geer]]), {{wt|Best Defense}} (1984, with [[Raye Birk]], [[David Paymer]], [[Paul Comi]], [[Gene Dynarski]], [[Paul Eiding]], [[Darryl Henriques]], [[John Hostetter]], and [[Joel Polis]]), and {{wt|The Best of Times (1986 film)|The Best of Times}} (1986, with [[Anne Haney]] and [[Tony Plana]]. Also that year, Dengel co-starred in {{wt|At Close Range}} with fellow "The Last Outpost" guest star [[Tracey Walter]] in their first work together. Dengel then acted in his first western, the 1988 telefilm ''The Tracker'' with [[Geoffrey Blake]], [[David Huddleston]], [[Mark Moses]], and [[Leon Rippy]]. Dengel's next telefilm role was 1989's ''Manhunt: Search for the Night Stalker'' with [[James Harper]] and [[Angela Paton]]. 

The 1990s found Dengel appearing in {{wt|Blind Faith (miniseries)|Blind Faith}} with [[David Andrews]], [[Jefrey Alan Chandler]], [[Gordon Clapp]], [[Aaron Lustig]], [[Dakin Matthews]], [[Marilyn Rockafellow]], [[Jimmie F. Skaggs]], [[Jay Underwood]], and Edward Wiley. Next Dengel rejoined Skaggs in {{wt|Lucky Chances}} with [[Stephanie Beacham]], [[Phil Morris]], and [[Tim Ryan]]. He also appeared in {{wt|Prayer of the Rollerboys}} (1990, with {{s|DS9}} star [[Aron Eisenberg]] and ''Deep Space Nine'' guest star [[Loren Lester]]), {{wt|Diary of a Hitman}} (1991, with [[Seymour Cassel]] and [[Brett Rickaby]]), ''Lady Boss'' (1992, with [[Jeff Austin]], [[Beth Toussaint]]-Coleman, [[Georgann Johnson]], and [[Nick Tate]]), {{wt|Four Eyes and Six Guns}} (1992, with [[John Schuck]]). In 1993 Dengel acted in ''The Contenders'' with [[Zach Grenier]].

In television, Dengel received a spot on {{wt|T. J. Hooker}} starring [[William Shatner]] and [[James Darren]]. Then Dengel was seen on {{wt|Hardcastle and McCormick}} starring [[Brian Keith]] and [[Daniel Hugh Kelly]] (1984). Dengel joined more ''Trek'' alumni on {{wt|Hill Street Blues}} starring [[Barbara Bosson]] and [[James B. Sikking]] (1986). They were joined by [[Joey Aresco]], [[Megan Gallagher]], and [[Steve Vinovich]].

Dengel next appeared on {{wt|Night Court}} starring [[John Larroquette]] (1987). That same year, Dengel had his last single guest work when he appeared on {{wt|LA Law}} starring [[Corbin Bernsen]] and [[Larry Drake]].
